brief_context: Location where the first atomic energy power station is built.
brief_extract: Just as fifty years ago the shape of the Comet airliner would not have been discerned in the Wright brothers' early flying machine, so even in the immediate pre-war period the possibility of atomic-fired power stations would not have been considered to be within the lifetime of the present generation. Today, however, it is announced that the first atomic energy power station is being built in Cumberland and, according to "The Times," in about two years' time it will be feeding electricity into the national grid. The new developments envisaged in so many fields will have their effects on men and women alike, and indeed women will be taking a part in bringing the benefits to the community.

brief_extract:
She runs government departments and manages innumerable businesses; she keeps factories going and still largely, though no longer entirely, trains and educates a nation's children."

"RETURN PASSAGE"
Miss Markham gives the reader a personal introduction to a way of life which has now vanished and to the men and women who helped to make this country great. She describes her girlhood in a Derbyshire Jacobean mansion ruled by an outwardly stern father and graced by her mother, an interesting and highly intelligent woman who came to maturity at a time when great ideas were stirring in the world, but whose tragedy it was that she had no one with whom to discuss them. Miss Markham's maternal grandmother was a woman of strong character and the wife of Joseph Paxton who, starting life as a gardener at a few shillings a week, became the architect of the Crystal Palace and died in 1865 leaving a fortune.

brief_context: The primary country discussed in the article.
brief_extract:
Thousands of young Turkish women now earn their living at clerical work. In building up the modern State of Turkey it was realised that trained and intelligent workers were needed with no artificial restrictions derived from their sex. THE ELECTRICAL AGE JANUARY, 1954
COMMENTARY
Humanity and Engineering
ELECTRICAL AGE readers would join in the chorus of good wishes given to Sir John Hacking, M.I.E.E., on his retirement from the office of Deputy Chairman (Operations) of the British Electricity Authority. A Lancastrian, Sir John has throughout his life taken an active part in those electrical engineering enterprises which contributed to this country's greatness, first on the North-East Coast, centre of some of our greatest engineering achievements, then in the Argentine supervising the electrification of the railways there, later in the U.S.A., South Africa and India again in connection with railway electrification, while he supervised the construction of the Grid in Mid-East and North-East England. He became Chief Engineer of the Central Electricity Board, and in 1952 was President of the Institution of Electrical Engineers.

Of special significance in between was the awakening of her social conscience at home by the sight of colliers on the “Paddy Mail” near Tapton; her first steps in public life were those of a school manager at Chesterfield, of which town she afterwards became Mayor and which throughout her life has provided a mirror of social change which it is more difficult to estimate on a national scale.

brief_extract: This talk was given by Mr. Leslie Thomson, B.Sc., of The Kingston Clinic, Edinburgh; he carried out fascinating experiments to show how electronics are used in industry and in the manufacture of certain appliances. Describing a valve used in wireless sets, he said that it had three components: (1) the filament made of tungsten wire which when heated gives off electrons in a kind of cloud; (2) the anode or metal plate which absorbs the electrons; and (b) between these two parts a perforated grid through which the electrons pass, and which controls their flow.

What electricity means to the different kinds of activities which make up life in the countryside will be illustrated in the E.A.W. Annual Conference at Torquay in May. Delegates from city and suburb, and from other rural areas will hear from Mr.

location_standardised: West Country, South West England, England, United Kingdom

brief_extract: F. Steward, C.B.E., Chairman of the South-Western Electricity Board, of what has been achieved in the West Country; they will hear from other speakers of how these electrical achievements benefit the day-to-day life of a traditional farming area; and from a young woman university lecturer in horticulture they will learn not only of what electricity has to offer this special department of rural activity, but they will realise from the individual achievements of Dr. Daphne Vince the part which women can take.

brief_context: Location of a planned special breeder-type atomic power plant.
brief_extract:
Atomic Energy and Electricity Generation
This issue of the magazine also tells of perhaps the most dramatic and reassuring news that science has had to bring us for some time, news that will vitally alter the standard of life of this country in the generations to come. It is the presentation of atomic energy as a practical possibility for electricity generation as told in the Government booklet "Britain's Atomic Factories" and as exemplified in the announcement by the Minister of Works to the House of Commons of the decision to build a special atomic power plant of the "breeder" type in the far North of Scotland. Very simply, this type of plant means that it creates more fuel than it uses up, so that fuel shortage will eventually be a thing of the past.

brief_extract:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE APRIL, 1954

Scientific Adventure—
Today and Tomorrow

The Story of Britain's Atomic Factories

By PHYLLIS THOMPSON

ATOMIC energy development in Great Britain once again emphasises the routine skill and the brilliance to overcome unexpected difficulties which have always characterised British engineers. The story to date creates new pride in our national engineering heritage, and the future points to a transformation of this country's economy.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding the potential generation of nuclear electrical power.
article_title: Scientific Adventure—Today and Tomorrow: The Story of Britain's Atomic Factories
brief_extract:
The present position is the result of the bold application by the engineer of the scientist's abstruse research. The future depends on the further practical experience of theoretical assumptions, but:

"These studies suggest that, if certain assumptions turn out to be valid, it might ultimately be possible completely to replace coal by nuclear fuel for the generation of electrical power in the United Kingdom. No precise figures can be given for the amount of coal that would be saved if this were possible, but an indication is provided by the British Electricity Authority's estimate that its total requirements are likely to increase to an annual rate of 63 million tons in the next fifteen years.

The
daily output of highly active
effluent is equivalent in activity
to several times the entire stock
of radium in the world’s hospi-

let it destroy itself by radioactive
decay in the ordinary course of
nature, and it is therefore stored
at Windscale. The medium active
effluent is stored and then dis-

to a level of activity laid down by
the Ministry of Health.

Extracts from the Caroline Haslett Trust Lecture given by MISS JOAN SHARP at the Institution of Electrical Engineers on 26th January, 1954, under the chairmanship of Sir Joseph Hallsworth, M.A., Chairman, North Western Electricity Board. The Organisation of Electricity Supply in Western Germany
Electricity is generated in hydro-electric, coal and peat-burning power stations.

brief_context: Refugees from this region were moving into Western Germany.
brief_extract: Development is rapid. One company reported an increase of 300% in the number of its consumers between 1950 and 1953, but the abnormal post-war conditions must be taken into account, and the influx of refugees from Eastern Germany brings problems. Off-peak tariffs are available for water-heating, the preparation of animal feeding stuffs and, in some cases, to factories.

brief_context: Location where the ship swung across the stream.
brief_extract: With her squat, modern funnel she shoots the bridges with a nonchalance denied to the older colliers, who must pull their funnels down to clear them. Just below Wandsworth Bridge the Dame Caroline swung across the stream, and on our arrival at the jetty she was tying up alongside with the ease and familiarity of a ship coming to a well-known berth. Already the gangway was down to meet us.

location_standardised: Hartland Point, Devon, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: A location mentioned in the ship's log-book regarding fog.
brief_extract: In the ship's log-book for the passage just completed I noticed several references to strong head winds and a heavy westerly swell. And, "for good measure," as the master put it, "fog from the Longships to Hartland Point." A different picture indeed from that up-river scene in the Thames when the Dame Caroline sweeps home with the tide (engines dead slow), looking as though she had never seen a westerly swell. The Dame Caroline carries 17 crew (including the master), who have most of them sailed with him since he took over the ship soon after she was launched at Aberdeen in 1949.

location_standardised: River Thames, London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom

brief_extract: "They know I'll be around in the morning to have a look," was the master's comment. Going aft, we found some of the crew in a small mess enjoying their first bit of relaxation since they came to London River. brief_extract: Her point of discharge is decided according to traffic conditions in the river. Perhaps the keynote to the life of a coasting collier was given by Captain Richmond when he said: "We live in a world of tides." Coming up-river, these colliers must leave the Lower Pool about 2 1/2 hours before high water to give them the right conditions for negotiating the bridges and berthing at their destinations. When coming down "light," then they must leave about 4 1/2 hours before high water in order to get under the bridges.

brief_context: Location where studies on heat removal were conducted.
brief_extract: The reactor can be treated as a furnace and the heat generated in it can be transferred to a conventional generating plant. Studies have been made at Harwell on how to remove the heat and convert it to electrical or mechanical energy, but the problem lies in the choice of the best methods in all cases. The conclusion of this fascinating story says that “nuclear fission offers the unique possibility of a furnace which, whilst generating heat, produces more of an equally efficient secondary fuel than it burns of the primary fuel.” Among the three types of atomic energy producers—power convertors, power producers, power breeders—it would appear to be the last-mentioned that will set up a continuing process whose effects will in the decades to come be felt throughout our national life.

brief_extract:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE JULY, 1954
FULL OF GOOD THINGS
WE hope that readers will find this Conference souvenir number of the magazine full of good things, for the delegates certainly found an abundance of pleasure and interest in the West Country Conference, where they studied at close hand the advantages of electricity in the countryside; indeed the beautiful weather enabled them to see it all to advantage. At the same time long drives over the moors and along winding country lanes gave them a glimpse of what life might be like in the winter without electricity.

brief_context: Location of a 17th Century farmhouse mentioned in the text.
brief_extract: As in the Conference, the good things of this July issue are varied, and show how electricity distributes its benefits on a wide scale, whether it is in the country cottage or the ancestral mansion, the old farmhouse or the modern horticultural nursery. It is perhaps an interesting coincidence that the Devonshire farmhouse and the Monmouthshire mansion both date from the 17th Century, and that their owners today are able to give a graphic personal description of the position before and after the installation of electricity. No record of a visit to the West Country would be complete without reference to the traditional good fare, which the countryfolk have enjoyed for generations.

Electrical Journal

THE 500 delegates who came from all over Britain to attend the 29th Annual Conference of the E.A.W. at Torquay from 17th-20th May will long remember the speeches and visits which threw new light on electricity in the countryside. It is only by personal contact that the implications of a problem can be understood, and thus there was a special significance in the first hand experiences related by a farmer's wife, a farm director, the Chairman of the Consultative Council, and a University lecturer in horticulture.

brief_extract:
Under the Line Rental scheme consumers pay annual charges additional to their ordinary tariffs, depending on the cost of the scheme and their use of electricity, but as the mains are taken into the remote areas the capital cost increases and the revenue declines. The National Approach
The problem of securing rural development in areas without an industrial load to balance it led to the Debate on the whole subject in the House of Commons in June 1953. It was decided to treat rural electrification as a national problem, financing it from the overall resources of the supply industry itself and, for a period of years at any rate, not seeking any outside help or Government subsidy.

brief_context: Area where rural electrification will take a few years longer.
brief_extract:
The New Programme
Through a bold and far-reaching programme it is hoped to provide mains electricity for 85 per cent of all farms, and almost every village and hamlet by 1968. The job will take a few years longer in South - West England and South Wales because of the nature of the territory and the size of the task. In the next five years electricity will be taken to a further 60,000 farms and 260,000 other rural premises, and in the South-West this will cover 5,000 farms and about 25,000 other rural premises.

brief_extract:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE JULY, 1954
West Country Industry
The Bovey Tracey Pottery Company’s Works
“NO wonder decorated pottery is the price it is” was the reaction of the members who were fortunate enough to visit the Bovey Tracey Pottery Company, when they saw the skill and care spent on the production of the many attractive tea and dinner sets, vases and ornaments of all kinds. Plates and saucers are made outside the mould — cups and bowls inside; jugs and teapots are cast, and the clay for them is differently mixed; these were some of the things learned in the first shops visited, where men were seen at electrically operated turn-tables moulding table and toilet ware at an incredible rate.

brief_context: Mentioned as where Mr. Ervine's father lived.
brief_extract: The alterations in the conditions of life had been so outstanding that if any person who died, as his father did, in 1886, were resurrected and set down in any modern city today, he would be frightened out of his wits. His father had never seen electric light, a motor car, an aeroplane, a submarine, although he lived in a great industrial city of the North of Ireland. The most remarkable change was, however, in the status of women.

THE ELECTRICAL AGE JULY, 1954

All these problems, when solved, will provide basic knowledge which can be plundered by fishermen and mariner alike.

brief_extract: Miss Gertrude L. Entwisle, A.M.I.E.E., is a modest, retiring person, who does not give the appearance of having made history when in 1915 she entered the Electrical Engineering Department of the British Westinghouse (now Metropolitan-Vickers) at Trafford Park as the first woman on the technical staff. In the 39 years since then she has quietly carried on her job as design engineer, and power station plant in many parts of the world, especially in Australia and New Zealand, includes machines which were designed by this pioneer woman in Britain.

brief_context: Location of a Roman defensive chain mentioned in text.
brief_extract:
Looking back on a life full of interest and fun, I bless my many friends — not least among them Electricity! BAMBURGH CASTLE

THE electric light which now shines out from Bamburgh Castle at night had a strange and far-distant predecessor, for the fortified place here was of Saxon origin, and very probably formed part of the Roman defensive chain up the East Coast. Since the 6th century, at least, domestic and warning lights have gleamed from this commanding site, lights lit by Saxon, Dane and Scot.

brief_context: Bebba was a Saxon Queen of Northumbria.
brief_extract: Now, with the original Keep of Henry II's day and the Great Kitchen, together with the restored walls, battlements and numerous apartments, one can realise why the Castle was regarded as so important a place by such well-known persons as King John who visited it, Edward I who imprisoned the Welsh princes here, and by Harry Hotspur who was Constable. Bamburgh's connection with women is of special interest, for the name Bebbanborough derived from Bebba, a Saxon Queen of Northumbria of the early 7th century. Some seven hundred years later, in 1330, Queen Philippa from Hainault, wife of Edward III and mother of the Black Prince, defended the Castle against the Scots, and Queen Elizabeth I ordered its overhaul in 1575.

brief_context: The previous location of the silk worm industry.
article_title: VISIT TO LULLINGSTONE CASTLE SILK WORM FARM
brief_extract: It is unique in housing the only silk worm farm of its kind; here the raw silk is spun for the Royal Coronation robes. Although the castle dates back to the 13th cen-tury, the silk worm industry is a modern institution, which was trans-ferred from Leatherhead in 1934. In the incubation room the tiny silk worm eggs, which are laid in August, weigh 40,000 to one ounce, and are hatched in May, when the mulberry comes into leaf.

article_title: VISIT TO LULLINGSTONE CASTLE SILK WORM FARM
brief_extract: Botolph is situated on the castle lawns. The nave is Norman and the church contains the smallest font in England enclosed in a wooden case. Another unusual feature is the finely moulded ceiling of Queen Anne period.

brief_context: Region interested in sports reports from the transmitting station.
brief_extract: The diesels are started by compressed air and then change over to fuel. Members saw what is known as a "quality" room which is used for occasional direct broadcasts of sports reports of particular interest to the Midlands, especially at week-ends. In this quality room, members were intrigued by the dual record turn-tables, each of which had an arm worked by parallel-tracking, of especial use in pin-pointing a particular spot on a record.
